lede: The mass of an electron and the distance to the Sun cannot share a page written out in full: one needs thirty zeros in front of its digits, the other eleven behind them. Standard form ends the zero-counting, writing every number as one digit, a decimal part, and a power of ten.
can: Convert between an ordinary number and standard form, either way.
Multiply and divide by handling the fronts and the powers separately.
Match the powers before adding or subtracting.

md: A number is in standard form when it looks like $a \times 10^{n}$ with $a$ between 1 and 10 and $n$ a whole number, positive or negative. The front number says what the digits are; the power says how far the decimal point has been slid, and which way. Sliding left makes the power go up, sliding right makes it go down.

prompt: Warm-up, one tap. Write $3 \times 10^{2}$ as an ordinary number.
explain: $10^{2}$ is 100, so this is $3 \times 100 = 300$. That is the whole of the idea; everything else in this lesson is bookkeeping on top of it.

text: What the two parts actually mean

md: A number is in standard form when it looks like $a \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le a < 10$ and $n$ a whole number.

prompt: In $a \times 10^{n}$, which values may the front number $a$ take?
options: From 1 up to but not including 10
answer: From 1 up to but not including 10
explain: One non-zero digit before the decimal point, so $1 \le a < 10$. That is what makes the form standard.

md:
The front number $a$ carries the **digits**. The power $n$ carries the **size**. They do different jobs, which is why $9 \times 10^{8}$ is nine hundred million and never 72 — the 8 is not something to multiply by, it is a count of how far the digits have been moved.
The reason the rule insists on $1 \le a < 10$ is that it makes the writing unique. Without it, $4\,830\,000$ could be written $48.3 \times 10^{5}$ or $0.483 \times 10^{7}$, and two numbers could no longer be compared by glancing at their powers.

prompt: Which of these is written in standard form?
explain: All three are the same number, $4\,830\,000$. Only the first has a front number between 1 and 10, and only that one counts as standard form on the answer line.

md:
To convert, slide the decimal point and count the places. Sliding **left** makes the front number smaller, so the power goes **up**. Sliding **right** makes it bigger, so the power goes **down** — which is where negative powers come from.
Count places, never zeros. That distinction is what saves you on a number such as $0.000\,062$, where the zeros and the places disagree.

prompt: Which of these is $4.7 \times 10^{-3}$ written as an ordinary number?
explain: A power of $-3$ slides the point three places left: $4.7 \rightarrow 0.47 \rightarrow 0.047 \rightarrow 0.0047$. Notice there are only two zeros after the point but three places moved.

md: Standard form is worth learning because it turns size into a single number you can read at a glance. Line the real world up by its powers of ten and the whole of physics and biology fits on one strip of paper.

caption: Every quantity here is one front number and one power. Comparing two of them starts with the power, and only goes to the front number when the powers tie.

explain: Compare the powers first: $-4$ is the furthest left on the line, so $9 \times 10^{-4}$ is smallest even though 9 is the biggest front number. The front number only decides a tie.

md:
The two halves are handled separately, and that is the whole method.
**1 Deal with the front numbers** — multiply them, or divide them.
**2 Deal with the powers** — add them when multiplying, subtract them when dividing. This is just the index law $10^{a} \times 10^{b} = 10^{a+b}$, which works because you are joining two runs of tens end to end.
**3 Re-normalise.** Step 1 often throws out a front number that is not between 1 and 10, so slide the point once more and adjust the power. $16 \times 10^{4}$ becomes $1.6 \times 10^{5}$; $0.4 \times 10^{2}$ becomes $4 \times 10^{1}$.

explain: $2 \times 4 = 8$ and $5 + (-2) = 3$, giving $8 \times 10^{3}$. The front number was already between 1 and 10, so no re-normalising was needed this time.

text: Adding and subtracting: match the powers first

md:
There is no index law for addition, and the examiners report that this is the part candidates find hardest by hand. You cannot add the front numbers unless the powers already agree, for the same reason you cannot add 3 metres to 4 centimetres without converting one of them.
So make the powers agree. Raise the smaller power to match the larger one, sliding that front number's point left to compensate, then add or subtract down the column and re-normalise.

explain: Rewrite $4 \times 10^{-4}$ as $0.4 \times 10^{-3}$, then $7.2 - 0.4 = 6.8$, giving $6.8 \times 10^{-3}$. Matching the powers turns a hard subtraction into an easy one.

explain: Rewrite $3 \times 10^{3}$ as $0.3 \times 10^{4}$, then $5 + 0.3 = 5.3$, giving $5.3 \times 10^{4}$. Adding the powers as well would give $8 \times 10^{7}$, which is more than a thousand times too big.

title: Standard Form - Corbettmaths
why: Ten minutes of conversions and calculations at the pace of someone writing them out by hand. Watch it once for the rhythm, then come back and do the gate below without pausing it.

prompt: Without scrolling back: which is $0.000\,000\,84$ in standard form?
explain: The point slides seven places right to sit after the 8, so the power is $-7$. Count places, not zeros — there are six zeros and seven places. The third option is the right size but its front number is not below 10.

md: Standard form makes two quantities look comparable even when they are not, and CCEA has exploited that twice in recent series. **A power of ten is not a unit.** If one mass is in grams and the other in kilograms, the powers are measuring different things and comparing them means nothing.

prompt: A question gives one length in metres and one in kilometres. What is your first written line?
options: The conversion of one length into the other's unit
The two powers of ten, compared
The difference between the two front numbers
answer: The conversion of one length into the other's unit
explain: It is the line the scheme rewards and the line that stops the trap. Comparing powers across different units compares nothing at all.

md: Convert first, to whichever unit you prefer, and write the conversion down. $1.05 \times 10^{7}$ grams is $1.05 \times 10^{4}$ kilograms, because dividing by 1000 lowers the power by 3.

prompt: $A = 3.4 \times 10^{5}$ grams and $B = 4 \times 10^{2}$ kilograms. Which is heavier?
explain: $A$ is $3.4 \times 10^{2}$ kg, or 340 kg, against $B$'s 400 kg. Comparing the printed powers, 5 against 2, points the wrong way, which is exactly the trap.

text: A percentage change on a standard-form number

md:
This is the question CCEA keeps setting, and the one that goes wrong most often. Nothing about the percentage is different because the number is in standard form: find the percentage of it, add it on or take it off, then **put the answer back into standard form**.
The last move is the one that gets forgotten. $9 \times 10^{8}$ increased by 30% gives $11.7 \times 10^{8}$, which is correct arithmetic and a lost mark, because $11.7$ is not between 1 and 10. Slide once more: $1.17 \times 10^{9}$.

prompt: $4 \times 10^{6}$ is increased by 50%. What is the new value?
explain: Half of $4 \times 10^{6}$ is $2 \times 10^{6}$, and $4 + 2 = 6$, so the answer is $6 \times 10^{6}$. Here the front number stayed inside the range; next time check rather than assume.

md:
Paper 2 lets you type these straight in, using the $\times 10^{x}$ key — not the $x^{y}$ key, and never by typing the digits $\times 10$ and then a power, which changes what the calculator does with brackets around it.
The display answers in one of two ways. Some calculators show $6.82 \times 10^{8}$ properly; others show **6.82E8** or **6.82 08**. Both mean the same thing, and neither is an answer. Copy it onto the answer line in full: $6.82 \times 10^{8}$. An E on an answer line earns nothing.

prompt: Your calculator display reads **4.5E-06**. What goes on the answer line?
explain: The E is the calculator's shorthand for times ten to the power. Write the power out properly. $4.5^{-6}$ is a completely different number, about $0.000\,11$.

text: Where the marks are actually lost

title: Summer 2025, M8 Paper 1 Q7 and M7 Paper 1 Q16
md: The same three-mark question, a 30% increase on a number in standard form, on both papers. On M8 over a third of candidates scored nothing and just under 40% scored all three. The reported failures were: finding the percentage and never adding it on, and leaving $1\,170\,000\,000$ sitting on the answer line after the question had asked for standard form.

prompt: You have reached $11.7 \times 10^{8}$ and the question said standard form. What do you write?
explain: All three are the same size. Only the first obeys $1 \le a < 10$, and the final mark is for the form, not the size.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the M7 and M8 formula sheet (page 2):** nothing for this topic. It carries the prism, trapezium, sphere and cone formulae, the quadratic formula and the trigonometric rules.
**Must be known:** $a \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le a < 10$; $10^{0} = 1$ and $10^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{10^{n}}$; $10^{a} \times 10^{b} = 10^{a+b}$ and $10^{a} \div 10^{b} = 10^{a-b}$; $(a \times 10^{n})^{k} = a^{k} \times 10^{nk}$; and the metric steps $1\text{ kg} = 10^{3}\text{ g}$, $1\text{ km} = 10^{3}\text{ m}$, $1\text{ g} = 10^{3}\text{ mg}$.

explain: Square both parts: $3^{2} = 9$ and $10^{4 \times 2} = 10^{8}$, giving $9 \times 10^{8}$. The power is multiplied by 2, not added to itself in the front number.

title: Why the units come before the arithmetic
md: Standard form makes two quantities look comparable when they are not: grams and kilograms sit side by side looking the same size. Converting one into the other's unit is what makes the two powers of ten mean the same thing.

prompt: You are stuck on a standard-form question with mixed units. What do you write first?
answer: the conversion | convert the units | convert to the same unit | the unit conversion | change to the same unit | put both in the same unit | same unit
explain: Put both quantities into one unit and write that line down. It scores on its own and it usually makes the rest of the question obvious.

md:
Keep the front number between 1 and 10.
Multiply and divide the fronts, add and subtract the powers.
Match the powers before adding or subtracting.
Convert the units before comparing anything.

One of four wordings: write a number in standard form, order three of them, calculate with two, or apply a percentage change to one. Mostly on the non-calculator paper. The last mark is nearly always for the **form** — an answer left as an ordinary number, or as $11.7 	imes 10^{8}$, drops it. Stuck: convert both quantities into the same unit first.
